purpose: Thyrotropin alfa is used to help doctors check for any remaining thyroid cancer cells after your thyroid has been removed. It is also used to help a radioactive iodine treatment work better to destroy any leftover thyroid tissue. This medication makes it easier for your doctor to get accurate test results without you having to stop your thyroid hormone replacement pills.
how_it_works: Your thyroid cancer cells need a signal called TSH to absorb iodine, which is used in both testing and treatment. This medication is a man-made version of that TSH signal. When you get this injection, it tells any remaining thyroid cancer cells to absorb iodine, making them show up clearly on scans or making them easier to destroy with radioactive iodine treatment.
common_side_effects: Nausea, headache, tiredness, vomiting, and dizziness are the most common side effects. Some people also feel flu-like symptoms or have mild discomfort at the injection site. These effects are usually short-lived and go away on their own.
warnings: In rare cases, this medication can cause swelling of remaining thyroid tissue, which could press on your airway and make breathing difficult — tell your doctor right away if you have trouble swallowing or breathing. People with certain types of thyroid cancer (metastatic) should be monitored carefully because swelling around tumors can be serious. Always tell your doctor about all your medications and any allergies before using this drug.
typical_dosing: This medication is given as two injections into the muscle (usually the buttock), 24 hours apart. Your doctor or nurse will give you these injections in a clinic or hospital. A radioactive iodine scan or treatment is then done 24 to 72 hours after the second injection.
